sentences.text: The known specimen of Scansoriopteryx heilmanni represents the remains of a hatchling maniraptoran dinosaur that was roughly the size of a sparrow.
The lower jaw of this animal contained at least twelve teeth, which were larger at the front than at the back.
Scansoriopteryx had a pubis that pointed forward, a primitive trait among theropods.
The creature possessed short legs covered in small pebbly scales, with possible impressions of long feathers on the upper foot.
It featured an unusually large first toe that may have been reversed to allow grasping.
An unusual, elongated third finger likely supported a membranous wing, with long feathers attaching to this digit rather than the middle one.
Unlike modern bird hatchlings, this species had forelimbs longer than its hind limbs.
The genus Scansoriopteryx was named by Czerkas and Yuan in 2002.
It is known from a single juvenile fossil specimen discovered in Liaoning, China.
Czerkas and Yuan initially reported that the Scansoriopteryx specimen likely came from the Yixian Formation.
Fossilized impressions of feathers are preserved on the type specimen of Scansoriopteryx.
The animal had a semilunate bone in the wrist allowing for bird-like folding motion in the hand.
Researchers interpreted the hallux of Scansoriopteryx as reversed, a condition common in modern tree-dwelling birds.
Researchers suggest Scansoriopteryx may have used its tail as a prop, similar to modern woodpeckers.
Czerkas and Yuan speculated that adults may have had wing feathers for leaping or gliding, but ruled out powered flight.
Researchers Czerkas and Yuan argued that Scansoriopteryx possessed primitive and birdlike characters that supported an unorthodox interpretation of dinosaur evolution.
Most researchers consider the genus Scansoriopteryx to be a synonym of Epidendrosaurus.
Scansoriopteryx is classified as a member of the clade Avialae and is considered a close relative of true birds.
The genus Scansoriopteryx gave its name to the family Scansoriopterygidae.
The fossil range of Scansoriopteryx spans from the Callovian to the Oxfordian stages.
The holotype skeleton of Epidendrosaurus was recovered from the Daohugou fossil beds in northeastern China.
The age of the Daohugou beds has been estimated anywhere from 169 million years ago in the Middle Jurassic to 122 million years ago in the Early Cretaceous.
The exact age of the Daohugou formation is debated because it affects understanding of Epidendrosaurus relationships and the origin of birds.
There is a scientific debate regarding whether Scansoriopteryx is a senior synonym or a junior synonym of the genus Epidendrosaurus.
The hypothesis that Scansoriopteryx evolved from non-dinosaurian archosaurs rather than being a dinosaur has been overwhelmingly rejected by paleontologists.
